newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela bolivar not greatly overvalued - official.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela bolivar not greatly overvalued - official.

text.p: High inflation rates and a stable exchange rate policy may have caused the Venezuelan bolivar to become somewhat overvalued, but there was no cause to expect a sharp depreciation, a top Central Bank official said Monday.

"When there is inflationary pressure and the exchange rate does not adjust exactly in line with that inflationary pressure there is overvaluation," Central Bank Director Domingo Maza Zavala told local Union Radio.
"But I don't think that it (overvaluation) is that large," he added.
Local businessmen have become increasingly critical of the Central Bank's strong bolivar policy in recent weeks saying it had led to about a 10 percent overvaluation of the currency.
Maza acknowledged that the Bank was using the exchange rate as a weapon in the fight against inflation, which hit 103.2 percent last year.
But he added that "it's not that the exchange rate is fixed or rigid, but rather stable within manageable limits which allow market forces to operate."

The Central Bank currently allows the currency to fluctuate 7.5 percent either side of a central rate. The central rate depreciates at 1.32 percent per month, in line with the government's inflation target.

"So there is no cause to expect a sharp depreciation of the exchange rate or a revaluation (appreciaton) but rather steady, normal, moderate progress within limits managed by the Central Bank," Maza said.
